knowledge_point.title: Applying the Fundamental Theorem of Line Integrals When the Potential Function Is Not Given

question.:question/problem:
Consider the curve $C$, traversed in the direction of increasing $t$, where

$$
r(t)=\langle t + 1,t + 2\rangle,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

Evaluate $\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r$ for $F(x,y)=\left(- 2 y\right)\,i+\left(- 2 x\right)\,j.$

*Hint: The field is conservative. Find a potential function, then subtract its value at the starting point from its value at the ending point.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
Write $P=- 2 y$ and $Q=- 2 x.$ A potential must satisfy $f_x=P$ and $f_y=Q$. Integrating the first component with respect to $x$ gives

$$
f(x,y)=- 2 x y+g(y)
$$

Match its $y$ derivative to the second component:

$$
\begin{aligned}- 2 x+g'(y)&=- 2 x \\ g'(y)&=0 \\ g(y)&=0+K\end{aligned}
$$

Choose $K=0$, since a constant cancels in the endpoint difference. Thus

$$
f(x,y)=- 2 x y
$$

Differentiating verifies both components of the given field. For the stated orientation, the starting and ending points are

$$
\begin{aligned}A&=(1,2) \\ B&=(2,3)\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the potential at each endpoint:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(B)&=- 2 \left(2\right) \left(3\right) \\ &=-12 \\ f(A)&=- 2 \left(1\right) \left(2\right) \\ &=-4\end{aligned}
$$

The fundamental theorem for line integrals gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r & =\int_C\nabla f\cdot\mathrm{d}r \\  & =f(B)-f(A) \\  & =\left(-12\right)-\left(-4\right) \\  & =-8.\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: Field smooth on R^2; path continuous on its given real interval.

knowledge_point.title: Applying the Fundamental Theorem of Line Integrals When the Potential Function Is Not Given

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=\left(2 x e^{- y}\right)\,i+\left(- x^{2} e^{- y} + 6 y\right)\,j.
$$

Evaluate $\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r$, where $C$ is the curve $y=\ln{\left(x - 3 \right)}$ for $x\in [4,5]$, traversed in the direction of decreasing $x$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Write $P=2 x e^{- y}$ and $Q=- x^{2} e^{- y} + 6 y.$ Both components have continuous partial derivatives on $\mathbb R^2$, and

$$
P_y=Q_x=- 2 x e^{- y}
$$

Since $\mathbb R^2$ is simply connected, the field is conservative. A potential must satisfy $f_x=P$ and $f_y=Q$. Integrating the first component with respect to $x$ gives

$$
f(x,y)=x^{2} e^{- y}+g(y)
$$

Match its $y$ derivative to the second component:

$$
\begin{aligned}- x^{2} e^{- y}+g'(y)&=- x^{2} e^{- y} + 6 y \\ g'(y)&=6 y \\ g(y)&=3 y^{2}+K\end{aligned}
$$

Choose $K=0$, since a constant cancels in the endpoint difference. Thus

$$
f(x,y)=x^{2} e^{- y} + 3 y^{2}
$$

Differentiating verifies both components of the given field. A parametrization is

$$
r(t)=\langle t,\ln{\left(t - 3 \right)}\rangle,\,t\in [4,5].
$$

For the stated orientation, the starting and ending points are

$$
\begin{aligned}A&=(5,\ln{\left(2 \right)}) \\ B&=(4,0)\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the potential at each endpoint:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(B)&=\left(4\right)^{2} e^{- \left(0\right)}+3 \left(0\right)^{2} \\ &=16 \\ f(A)&=\left(5\right)^{2} e^{- \left(\ln{\left(2 \right)}\right)}+3 \left(\ln{\left(2 \right)}\right)^{2} \\ &=3 \ln{\left(2 \right)}^{2} + \frac{25}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

The fundamental theorem for line integrals gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r & =\int_C\nabla f\cdot\mathrm{d}r \\  & =f(B)-f(A) \\  & =\left(16\right)-\left(3 \ln{\left(2 \right)}^{2} + \frac{25}{2}\right) \\  & =\frac{7}{2} - 3 \ln{\left(2 \right)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here $e^{-\ln(1)}=1$ and $e^{-\ln(2)}=\frac{1}{2}$.

knowledge_point.title: Applying the Fundamental Theorem of Line Integrals When the Potential Function Is Not Given

question.:question/problem:
Consider the curve $C$, traversed in the direction of decreasing $t$, where

$$
r(t)=\langle \ln{\left(t \right)},t^{2}\rangle,\,t\in [1,3].
$$

Evaluate $\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r$ for $F(x,y)=\left(- x^{2} - 3 y\right)\,i+\left(- 3 x + y^{2}\right)\,j.$

*Hint: You may wish to use the fact that $F$ is conservative.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
Write $P=- x^{2} - 3 y$ and $Q=- 3 x + y^{2}.$ A potential must satisfy $f_x=P$ and $f_y=Q$. Integrating the first component with respect to $x$ gives

$$
f(x,y)=- \frac{x^{3}}{3} - 3 x y+g(y)
$$

Match its $y$ derivative to the second component:

$$
\begin{aligned}- 3 x+g'(y)&=- 3 x + y^{2} \\ g'(y)&=y^{2} \\ g(y)&=\frac{y^{3}}{3}+K\end{aligned}
$$

Choose $K=0$, since a constant cancels in the endpoint difference. Thus

$$
f(x,y)=- \frac{x^{3}}{3} - 3 x y + \frac{y^{3}}{3}
$$

Differentiating verifies both components of the given field. For the stated orientation, the starting and ending points are

$$
\begin{aligned}A&=(\ln{\left(3 \right)},9) \\ B&=(0,1)\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the potential at each endpoint:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(B)&=- \frac{\left(0\right)^{3}}{3}+\frac{\left(1\right)^{3}}{3}- 3 \left(0\right) \left(1\right) \\ &=\frac{1}{3} \\ f(A)&=- \frac{\left(\ln{\left(3 \right)}\right)^{3}}{3}+\frac{\left(9\right)^{3}}{3}- 3 \left(\ln{\left(3 \right)}\right) \left(9\right) \\ &=- 27 \ln{\left(3 \right)} - \frac{\ln{\left(3 \right)}^{3}}{3} + 243\end{aligned}
$$

The fundamental theorem for line integrals gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r & =\int_C\nabla f\cdot\mathrm{d}r \\  & =f(B)-f(A) \\  & =\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)-\left(- 27 \ln{\left(3 \right)} - \frac{\ln{\left(3 \right)}^{3}}{3} + 243\right) \\  & =- \frac{728}{3} + \frac{\ln{\left(3 \right)}^{3}}{3} + 27 \ln{\left(3 \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$
